title: Nearly Optimal Fixed-Confidence Best-Arm Identification with 1-Bit Feedback
claim: Our estimator achieves lower error than the prior estimator and its bias floor is far smaller, though both floor under heavy tails.
layout: 3 panels in a row, shared legend below, log-log error curves
description: Three side-by-side log-log line plots titled Normal, Student-t (df=5) and Exponential. The x-axis is the number of samples n, from about 10 to 10^7. The y-axis is mean absolute error E|mu_hat_n - mu|, from 10^-3 to 10^0. In each panel an orange line (our estimator) sits below a blue line (Lau–Scarlett), each with a shaded band for standard deviation. Both lines fall along a grey dashed O(1/sqrt n) reference. A green dotted horizontal line marks the theoretical bias upper bound. Dashed orange and blue horizontal lines show the true bias floors. In the Normal panel the curves keep falling. In the heavy-tailed panels they flatten at their bias floors, and ours flattens lower. One shared legend box sits below all three panels. The eye goes first to the orange-versus-blue gap.
caption: Mean absolute error E|ˆµn −µ| over the number of 1-bit queries n for our estimator and the estimator of [21] (mean ± std over runs). For readability, bias lines below 10−3 are not shown.
abstract: We study fixed-confidence best-arm identification under strict 1-bit feedback constraints. At each round, the learner selects an arm and a query set, and receives only a single bit indicating whether the sampled reward belongs to that set. We consider a distribution-free finite-variance setting with arm-wise localization, where direct empirical mean estimation is no longer available and clipping becomes unavoidable. We first formulate a time-uniform 1-bit mean-estimation primitive based on randomized threshold queries and a clipped tail-integral identity. We then embed this primitive into candidate-challenger best-arm identification algorithms. A fixed-clipping algorithm gives a simple anytime $(Îµ,Î´)$-PAC guarantee, while a phased adaptive-clipping algorithm matches the clipping level to the current resolution and yields a gap-adaptive sample complexity. We also prove a $K$-arm worst-case information-theoretic lower bound showing that the logarithmic penalty caused by finite-variance 1-bit feedback is intrinsic. This bound matches the leading dependence of the phased algorithm up to logarithmic factors.
